INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE
The Commonwealth of Virginia has an interest in
ensuring the safety of its citizens.   Its elected
representatives have chosen to promote public safety
by restricting the purchase and sale of assault
firearms.  Va. Code § 18.2-287.4:1; see Va. Code
§ 18.2-308.2:2(F) (defining “assault firearm”).
Multiple courts have stayed lawsuits challenging
Virginia’s assault-firearms laws pending this Court’s
resolution of these cases.  See, e.g. , Order at 1,
McDonald v. Katz, No. 1:26-cv-1305 (E.D. Va. July 24,
2026).
STATEMENT
Since shortly after the AR -15 platform and the
other assault weapons at issue in this appeal
(collectively AR -15s, for ease of reference), became
broadly available to American consumers, states have
restricted their possession .  California enacted the
first such law  in 1989.  See Cal. Penal Code § 12280
(1989), Cal. Stat. 1989, c h. 19  (now codified at Cal.
Penal Code § 30600).  At the time,  by one estimate,
manufacturers produced a modest “average of 91,000
guns annually” in “five categories of assault weapons,”
including AR-15s.  U.S. Dep ’t of Just ., Off . of Just .
Programs, Impacts of the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban:
1994–96 at 4 –5, available at https://perma.cc/JZA6-
DKPY.
Several states followed suit before the federal
government imposed a national  ban in 1994.  See
Pub. L. 103 -322, § 110102, 108 Stat. 1796 (1994) .
When the ban expired  in 2004 , five states and the
District of Columbia independently restricted AR-15s.
Still other states enacted restrictions in the following
years.

2
Earlier this year, Virginia enacted Senate Bill 749,
which, among other things, makes it a crime to buy or
sell an assault firearm, subject to certain exceptions
and a grandfather clause.  See Va. Code
§ 18.2-287.4:1(B)–(C).
Multiple plaintiffs sued in local and federal
Virginia courts.  Two Virginia circuit courts issued
preliminary injunctions restricting enforcement of the
challenged laws, including one with statewide
application.  See Order at 1 –2, Crump v. Katz , No.
CL26000201-00 ( Lancaster Cnty. Cir. Ct. June 30,
2026); Order at 2 –3, Santolla v. Katz , No.
CL26001139-00 (Wash. Cnty. Cir. Ct. July 9, 2026).
Later, those courts and all the other courts
entertaining similar challenges issued stays pending
the outcome of these writs of certiorari.1
Today, 1 1 states and the District of Columbia —
collectively representing over 34 percent of the United
States’ population—have laws restricting AR-15
possession.2

1 See Order at 1–2, Crump, No. CL26000201-00 (Sept. 10, 2026);
Order, Santolla, No. CL26001139-00 (July 28, 2026); Order at 2,

(6) (693,645); 720 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/24 -1.9(b)–(c) (12,719,141);
Md. Code, Crim. Law § 4-303 (6,265,347); Mass. Gen. Laws ch.
140, § 131M (7,154,084); N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 2C:39-1(w), 2C:39-5(f)

3
SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
AR-15s are not “ Arms” that the Second
Amendment protects.  A state may therefore choose to
restrict its citizens’ ability to possess such weapons.
This Court has already recognized that states may
restrict machinegun possession.  District of Columbia
v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 627 (2008).  Machineguns are
not “Arms” because they are dangerous and inapt for
self-defense.  AR-15s are machineguns, except that
they—at least to start —have semiautomatic fire
rather than automatic fire.  AR-15s thus bear nearly
all the same features that take machineguns outside
the Second Amendment’s protection.
Even if the difference between automatic fire and
semiautomatic fire were enough to change the
dangerousness determination, several inexpensive
and inconspicuous  devices exist to turn a
semiautomatic assault rifle into a machinegun or its
functional equivalent.  This Court should not ignore
these realities in assessing AR-15s’ dangerousness.
Petitioners bore the burden to establish that
AR-15s are “ Arms” within the Second Amendment ’s
protection. Their showing before this Court  suffers
from multiple flaws.  They ask this Court to rely on
statistics extrapolated from gun-owner surveys, none

(9,548,215); N.Y. Penal Law § § 265.00(22), 265.02(7)
(20,002,427); R.I. Gen. Laws § 11-47.2 (1,114,521); Va. Code
§ 18.2-287.4:1 (8,880,107); Wash. Rev. Code § § 9.41.010(2),
9.41.240; 9.41.390. (8,001,020); see also U.S. Census Bureau,
Population Div., Annual Estimates of the Resident Population for
the United States, Regions, States, District of Columbia, and
Puerto Rico: April 1, 2020 to July 1, 2025 (NST -EST2025-POP)
(Jan. 2026), available at https://perma.cc/G2KE-RYPX.

4
of which  shows actual use .  They ask this Court to
focus on the stocks and grips of AR -15s while
downplaying the tremendous lethality of these
weapons.  And they ask this Court to adopt a
methodology for deciding when a weapon is a Second
Amendment “arm” that turns on recent legislative
and consumer happenstance.  The constitutionality of
states’ assault-weapons laws, and the safety of
millions of Americans, should not depend on such
contingencies.
ARGUMENT
I. AR-15s are not Second Amendment
protected “Arms.”
A. Bruen step one and step two differ in
which party bears the burden.
The Second Amendment provides that “the right of
the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be
infringed.”  Its protection “ applies equally to the
Federal Government and the States .”  McDonald v.
City of Chicago , 561 U.S. 742, 791 (2010)  (citation
omitted).  This Court has “identified the Amendment’s
‘central’ concern: securing the fundamental right of
self-defense.”  Wolford v. Lopez , 609 U.S. 185, 192
(2026) (citation omitted ).  T he right secured by the
Second Amendment is not unlimited ; instead, it
“protects a right that already existed” at adoption.  Id.
at 193 (citations omitted); see id. at 196 (the “right was
not in every way coterminous with the Amendment ’s
literal language”).
After New York State Rifle & Pistol Assoc ., Inc. v.
Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022 ), courts conduct a two -step
analysis of Second Amendment challenges to statutes.
See Wolford, 609 U.S. at 195.  At the first step, a court

5
determines whether the challenged law “clashes with
the ‘plain text ’ of the Amendment ’s language ” by
asking “ three subsidiary questions .”  Id. (citation
omitted).  The challenger bears the burden of
establishing whether the law applies to “the people”;
whether “ it concern [s] any form of ‘Arms’”; and
whether it restricts either the keeping or bearing of
arms.  See i d. (citations omitted).  If the answer to
each question is “yes,” then the law “is presumptively
unconstitutional.”  Id. at 196 (citation omitted).
As to what constitutes protected “ Arms,” this
Court has recognized that the Second Amendment
protects only “ the sorts of weapons ” that were “in
common use at the time” of adoption.  Heller, 554 U.S.
at 627 (quoting United States v. Miller, 307 U.S. 174,
179 (1939)).  And it does not protect “ the carrying of
‘dangerous and unusual weapons. ’”  Id. (citations
omitted).  Instead, “t he Second Amendment ’s
definition of ‘arms’ . . .  covers modern instruments
that facilitate armed self-defense.”  Bruen, 597 U.S. at
28 (citation omitted).
On the unprotected side of the line are “M-16 rifles
and the like ,” and “short-barreled shotguns.” Heller,
554 U.S. at 625, 627 .  On the protected side are
handguns, “ the quintessential self -defense weapon .”
Id. at 629.  That said, this Court has not established
“a comprehensive framework for evaluating
restrictions on types of weapons,” including for how to
assess “what makes a weapon ‘bearable,’ ‘dangerous,’
or ‘unusual.’”  Harrel v. Raoul, 144 S. Ct. 2491, 2492
(2024) (Thomas, J., statement respecting denial of
certiorari).
At the second step of the analysis, the “ relevant
government” entity defending the la w can show that

6
the law “did not infringe the historical understanding
of the codified right. ”  Wolford, 609 U.S. at 196
(citation omitted).  It can rely on “ [a] variety of
sources, including scholarship,” but, often, proffering
one or more “historical analogues” is the best evidence
that the current law does not infringe historical
understandings.  Id. (citations omitted).
The Commonwealth agrees with respondents’
Bruen step two analysis.  See Grant Resp. Br. 9 –23;
Viramontes Resp. Br. 13–25. This amicus brief focuses
on Bruen step one, but the points it makes below apply
equally if the Court analyzes common use and
dangerousness at Bruen step two.
B. AR-15s are not protected because they
are dangerous and inapt for self -
defense.
1. AR-15s are exceedingly similar to
unprotected machineguns.
AR-15s are  not “ the sorts of weapons . . .  ‘in
common use at the time’” of the Second Amendment’s
adoption.  Heller, 554 U.S. at 627  (citation omitted).
Rather, they are not in common use for lawful
“individual self -defense” id. at 599, and they are
extraordinarily dangerous.
1. The simplest way to approach this question is to
recognize that consumers have multiple easy -toimplement—and hard -to-detect—options to convert
AR-15s to unprotected machineguns  or their
functional equivalent.  See Garland v. Cargill , 602
U.S. 406, 411 (2024)  (“Shooters have devised
techniques for firing semiautomatic firearms at rates
approaching those of some machineguns.”).

7
Bump stocks.   Bump stocks allow user s to
dramatically increase the rate of fire compared to a
stock AR-15.  A bump stock “replaces a semiautomatic
rifle’s stock . . . with a plastic casing that allows every
other part of the rifle to slide back and forth,” and “has
a ledge to keep the shooter’s trigger finger stationary.”
Cargill, 602 U.S. at 411–12.  This assists with “bump
firing,” where a shooter “ uses the firearm ’s recoil to
help rapidly manipulate the trigger .”  Id. at 411.  “A
rifle equipped with a bump stock can fire at a rate
between 400 and 800 rounds per minute.”  Id. at 434
(Sotomayor, J., dissenting).  While this configuration
does not meet the technical definition of a
“machinegun” under the National Firearms Act, id. at
410, it is no less deadly than one in practice.  Indeed,
“[t]he horrible shooting spree in Las Vegas in
2017 . . . demonstrated that a semiautomatic rifle
with a bump stock can have the same lethal effect as
a machinegun.”  Id. at 429 (Alito, J., concurring); see
also Bianchi v. Brown , 111 F.4th 438, 456 (4th Cir.
2024) (en banc), cert. denied sub nom. Snope v. Brown,
145 S. Ct. 1534 (2025).
Auto sears.  Auto sears are small firearm parts that
turn AR -15s into fully automatic machineguns.  By
default, an AR-15 will load and fire one cartridge per
trigger pull, because a small hook on an internal part
called a “disconnector” will catch the hammer as it
moves backwards in the firing sequence.  Cargill, 602
U.S. at 420.  To reinitiate the firing sequence, the
shooter must pull the trigger again.  Id. at 416, 420.
By contrast, “[t]he auto sear catches the hammer as it
swings backwards, but will release it again once a new
cartridge is loaded if the trigger is being held back .”
Id. at 420 n.4 (citation omitted) .  This means that
changing out a small internal component of the

8
AR-15, see id . at 417 –420 (illustrations of the
assembly), will make it a machinegun.
Auto sears are too easily made and installed to be
susceptible to effective enforcement.  They “c an be
made of plastic or metal  . . .  . are inexpensive[,] and
can be purchased online, oftentimes disguised as
harmless items, such as a Lego. ”  Manhattan Dist .
Att’ys Off., D.A. Bragg, Senator Hoylman -Sigal and
Assemblymember Rosenthal Announce New Push to
Address Emergence of 3D-Printed Guns & Auto Sears
(May 16, 2025), available at https://perma.cc/5DH8-
4P5F.  With widespread blueprint availability, auto
sears can be 3 -D printed using a home setup for a
marginal cost of $5.00.  Id.
Even cruder, some end users have simply filed off
or otherwise removed the stock AR -15 disconnector
hook, ostensibly in an effort to make the weapon fully
automatic.  See Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms,
and Explosives, National Firearms Act Handbook,
Appendix B  at 1 –2, available at
https://perma.cc/E4JP-QZTD (noting that many
AR-15s, even when not fully modified with M16
components, “ will also shoot automatically by
manipulation of the selector or removal of the
disconnector”).
Forced-reset triggers.   Forced-reset triggers  “are
aftermarket firearm components that allow a shooter
to maintain continuous pressure and achieve a
significantly higher rate of fire while technically
performing a separate trigger pull for each round.”  In
re Super Safety Pat. Litig., 829 F. Supp. 3d 1370, 1372
(U.S. Jud. Pan. Mult. Lit. 2026).  In short, they allow
shooters to continuously fire AR -15s simply by
maintaining enough pressure on the trigger.  See

9
United States v. Rare Breed Triggers, LLC , 690 F.
Supp. 3d 51, 64 (E.D.N.Y. 2023).  They allow “even a
novice shooter  . . . to fire multiple rounds of
ammunition in a fraction of a second.”  Id. at 65.
After initially taking the position that such devices
are illegal machinegun-conversion devices, see Rare
Breed Triggers , 690 F. Supp. 3d at 58, the federal
government eventually reversed course and ended
several enforcement efforts, see U.S. Dep’t  of Just .,
Off. of Pub. Affairs, Department of Justice Announces
Settlement of Litigation Between the Federal
Government and Rare Breed Triggers (May 16, 2025),
available at https://perma.cc/EJP4-BAXE.
These devices proliferated even before the federal
government stopped regulating them.   In the Rare
Breed Triggers case alone, the manufacturer had sold
“approximately 100,000” forced-reset triggers in less
than three years.  690 F. Supp. 3d at 58.  That means
AR-15s throughout the country have devices that
“mak[e] a weapon fire successive  rounds extremely
rapidly.”  Id. at 59.
Binary Triggers.   Binary triggers “shoot[] one
round of ammunition with each pull and each release
of the trigger.”  Rare Breed Triggers, 690 F. Supp. 3d
at 97 n.37. This “allow[s] for more rapid shooting than
a standard trigger.”  Id. The federal government does
not regulate these devices.  See id.
That end users would have to take some simple
steps to turn their AR-15s into machineguns does not
change the calculus .  As this Court recognized in
Bondi v. VanDerStok, both starter guns and firearm -
conversion kits are firearms under federal law .  604
U.S. 458, 471, 473 (2025).  This is so, despite the fact

10
that neither object can, in its present form, discharge
a projectile by means of an explosive, because “a
person without any specialized knowledge can convert
a starter gun [or a firearm -conversion kit] into a
working firearm using everyday tools in less than an
hour.”  Id. at 472 (citation omitted).  In common usage,
“artifact nouns ”—such as “weapon” or
“machinegun”—“sometimes capture unfinished
articles.”  Id. at 473 (citation omitted).  The same logic
applies here: AR -15s are not meaningfully less
dangerous than machineguns just because “ a person
without any specialized knowledge,” id. at 472, would
have to take a few easy steps to make the switch.  Cf.
Cargill, 602 U.S. 429 (Alito, J., concurring) (Congress
“would not have seen any material difference between
a machinegun and a semiautomatic rifle equipped
with a bump stock”).
Hewing to precedent with a full picture of AR-15s
yields a straightforward result: the Second
Amendment does not prevent states from restricting
AR-15s, just as with their fraternal twin, the
machinegun.  Heller, 554 U.S. at 627.
2. The federal government, as amicus, wrongly
asks this Court to hold that all firearms are, by
definition, Second Amendment-protected “Arms,” and
to proceed to Bruen step two “ without further ado .”
Fed. Gov’t Br. 8 –9.  This must be, it says, because
anything less “defies both the plain meaning of ‘arms’
and Heller’s interpretation of that term.”  Id. at 8.  But
the federal government ’s theory of the framework
leads to absurd results.
Judicially created tests should make some common
sense.  Interpreting the Bruen test to require holding
that laws regulating  weapons “such as the M16, the

11
short-barreled shotgun, the ricin pellet -firing
umbrella gun, and the W54 nuclear warhead ,”
Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 460, are “presumptively
unconstitutional,” subject to a government’s ability to
produce satisfactorily similar historical analogues,
Wolford, 609 U.S. at 196, defies common sense.  It
wrongly and automatically flips the burden to the
government to defend even the most frivolous
challenges.  And it wastes judicial resources by
requiring time-intensive history -and-tradition
analyses for each challenge.
The subparts of judicially created tests should each
do some work , too .  If all firearms are necessarily
“Arms,” as the federal government would have it, then
the second of the “ three subsidiary questions ” at
Bruen step one, Wolford, 609 U.S. at 195 , would do
nothing.  Litigants are not raising Second
Amendment challenges to arbitration clauses and
campaign-finance regulations; they are raising them
to restrictions on  firearms.  Asking the “Arms”
question, then, presumes that there is some subset of
arms that are not Second Amendment -protected
“Arms” at Bruen step one.
The question is how to go about deciding whether
the type of firearm at issue is such an “arm.”  This
Court should eschew the simplistic counting exercise
that petitioners suggest and instead focus on whether
a firearm’s characteristics make it unlike “the sorts of
weapons” that were “in common use at the time”  of
adoption.  Heller, 554 U.S. at 627.

12
2. AR-15s are not in common use for
lawful self-defense.
Petitioners misconstrue Heller’s common-use test.
Heller was clear about two things: First, lawful self -
defense is “the central component of the right itself ,”
554 U.S. at 599  (emphasis omitted) ; second, the
Second Amendment protects “ the sorts of weapons”
that were “in common use at the time” of adoption, id.
at 627  (emphasis added , citation omitted ).  Both
aspects undermine petitioners ’ focus on current
popularity.
1. To start, petitioners’ counting exercise (at 34 –
36) is untethered from the use of these weapons for
lawful self -defense.  Petitioners rely on surveys to
posit that millions of Americans own AR-15s, and that
manufacturers have made millions of them.  Pet’rs’
Br. 34–35.  Petitioners also rely on surveys for owners’
self-reports about why they own AR -15s. Id. at 35.
But none of this—even if accurate and properly before
the Court—shows that AR-15s are commonly used for
lawful self-defense.
On the contrary, usage data confirms how rarely
these arms are used defensively  compared to the
handgun—the “quintessential” self -defense weapon .
Heller, 554 U.S. at 629.  In one study, rifles generally
comprised four percent of defensive firearm uses,
compared to 90 percent for handguns. Grant Resp. Br.
32 (citation omitted). And FBI data covering more
than 20 years and 400 active -shooter incidents
revealed only one instance of a civilian intervening
with an assault weapon. Id. at 32 –33 (citation
omitted).

13
In any event, counting the numbers of AR-15s in
circulation is misleading. These guns are
concentrated in a small proportion of the gun-owning
population, and a smaller fraction of the American
populace. See William English, 2021 National
Firearms Survey: Updated Analysis Including Types
of Firearms Owned 33 (Georgetown McDonough Sch.
of Bus. Research Paper No. 4109494, 2022), available
at https://perma.cc/W7FG-493D (reporting that 30.2
percent of gun owners had ever owned an AR-15-style
rifle). And, to the extent AR-15s see actual use, the
evidence ties it to more mass shooters than to lawful
self-defense incidents .  See Christopher S. Koper et
al., Criminal Use of Assault Weapons and High -
Capacity Semiautomatic Firearms: An Updated
Examination of Local and National Sources , 95 J.
URB. HEALTH 313, 317 –19 (2018) , available at
https://perma.cc/9UC7-Q77R (finding assault
weapons disproportionately represented in mass
murders, particularly public mass shootings).
Petitioners place too much weight on this Court ’s
statements in Staples v. United States, 511 U.S. 600,
612–14 (1994), and Smith & Wesson Brands, Inc. v.
Estados Unidos Mexicanos, 605 U.S. 280, 297 (2025).
Staples construed the mens rea requirement of a
federal criminal statute.  511 U.S. at 604–05.  This
Court rejected the federal government ’s broad
argument that “ all guns  . . .  are dangerous devices
that put gun owners on notice that they must
determine at their hazard whether their weapons
come within the scope of the Act .”  Id. at 608.  “Guns
in general” are unlike grenades, narcotics, and waste
material, which put their owners on notice of their
dangers to the public.  Id. at 611–12.  Rather, guns as
a general category “ have been widely accepted as

14
lawful possessions” and so their mere possession was
insufficient to satisfy the mens rea requirement of the
federal statute at issue. Id. at 612.
Staples’ discussion of “[g]uns in general,” 511 U.S.
at 611, plainly has nothing to do with whether AR-15s
specifically are in common use.  On the contrary, this
Court would have “surely classif [ied] certain
categories of guns —no doubt including the
machineguns, sawed-off shotguns, and artillery pieces
that Congress has subjected to  regulation—as items
the ownership of which would have the same quasi -
suspect character we attributed to owning hand
grenades in [United States v. Freed , 401 U.S. 601
(1971)].”  Id. at 612.  This Court issued Staples in May
1994, and the federal assault-weapons ban took effect
in September.  Had Staples been decided the following
term, this Court “no doubt” would have added assault
weapons to the list of quasi -suspect weapons “ that
Congress has subjected to regulation.”  Id.
Smith & Wesson  is further afield from the issues
here.  There, this Court determined that a civil
complaint by the Mexican government against
American gun manufacturers did not plausibly allege
that the manufacturers had aided and abetted
unlawful gun use by third parties .  605 U.S. at 284 ,
287.  In noting that AR -15s might appeal to both
criminals and non -criminals, this Court, in two
sentences, stated that AR -15s and other “military
style” weapons “ are both widely legal and bought by
many ordinary consumers ” and that “[t] he AR-15 is
the most popular rifle in the country .”  Id. at 612
(citation omitted).  It is “inconceivable” that this Court
“would rest [its] interpretation . . .  upon such . . .
dictum in a case” where “[n] o Second Amendment

15
claim was raised or briefed by any party.”  Heller, 554
U.S. at 625 n.25.  These dicta are no substitute for
competent evidence of the AR -15’s actual usage for
lawful self-defense.
2. No number of present-day purchases can change
the fact that AR -15s are nothing like “the sorts of
weapons” in use in the late 18th century.  In the
Founding era, 50 to 60 percent of households owned a
firearm, typically a single -shot, muzzle -loading long
gun. J.A. 332.  AR-15s, by contrast,  are modern
weapons of war that would have been wholly foreign
to the framers of the Second Amendment.  They were
developed for Cold War battlefields in the 1950s and
1960s. Grant Resp. Br. 29 (citations omitted).  They
retain the muzzle velocity, range, and lethality
engineered to kill at hundreds of yards . Id. at 24–25
(citations omitted). And the rate at which they fire
rounds, Cargill, 602 U.S. at 433  (Sotomayor, J.,
dissenting) (60 –180 rounds per minute  without
modifications), would have baffled the framers.
Those features make them unnecessary and even
counterproductive for civilian self-defense.  See Bruen,
597 U.S. at 28  (“the Second Amendment [] . . . covers
modern instruments that facilitate armed self -
defense”) (emphasis added, citation omitted).  An AR-
15-compatible round meant to wound at battlefield
distances risks over -penetrating walls and
endangering bystanders , neighbors, and others in
one’s home.  See Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 458 .  In the
NRA’s Armed Citizen data, defenders fired 2.2 shots
on average and only 0.3  percent of defenders  fired
more than ten; in a systematic sample of news -
reported incidents, 97.3  percent fired five or fewer,
and none fired more than ten.  See Oregon Firearms

16
Fed’n, Inc. v. Kotek , 682 F. Supp. 3d 874, 896 –97 (D.
Or. 2023 ) ( discussing these data ); see also  Vermont
Fed’n of Sportsmen’s Clubs v. Birmingham , 741 F.
Supp. 3d 172, 191–97 (D. Vt. 2024).
3. Finally, f ocusing on current popularity is just
plain arbitrary.  The strength of popularity-based
Second Amendment challenges turn on contingencies
having nothing to do with the animating concerns of
the Second Amendment.  For example, assuming the
number of AR -15 owners increases every year, then
the constitutionality of states ’ regulations of AR-15s
will depend on the calendar year in which the
challenger filed his lawsuit.  California’s law was
certainly constitutional when passed in 1989 because
AR-15s were not then in common use.  It makes little
sense to have a test whereby the consumer
preferences of gun owners in other states slowly erode
the constitutionality of a longstanding law.
Conversely, a popularity focus  implies that types
of firearms may be banned if they fall  enough in
popularity before a court enshrines their protection,
or if they  never become popular in the first place.
This, too, has little connection to the central concerns
of the Second Amendment.
Popularity also turns on legislative happenstance.
Imagine, as a counterfactual, that Congress had
continued to renew the federal assault -weapons ban
until the present day.  There can be little doubt that
AR-15s would not be commonly owned in that
scenario, and thus presumably not protected by the
Second Amendment.   But that makes the
constitutionality of Cook County ’s and Connecticut’s
laws contingent on the existence, not the validity, of
federal legislation.  That makes little sense.

17
Petitioners also imply that the constitutionality of
states’ AR-15 laws is suspect because AR -15s “ are
legal in the vast majority of the states .”   Pet’rs’ Br.
35.  But simply tallying the number of states that
have enacted similar legislation misses important
context.  For example, petitioners do not acknowledge
that the 11 regulating states and the District of
Columbia comprise more than a third of the United
States’ population.  See supra at 2 –3 n.2.  And it
ignores the trend in which states enact AR-15
restrictions much more frequently than they repeal
them.  Petitioners’ theory invites arbitrariness by
incentivizing freezing states ’ abilities to enact these
regulations before a critical mass has done so.  Would
Heller have come out the other way had a large
majority of states imposed a similar  good-cause
regime to D.C. ’s at the time of Heller ’s lawsuit?
Petitioners’ theory suggests that it should have.  See
Pet’rs’ Br. 35.
In any event, the notion that some states’ decisions
to not restrict AR -15s affects the constitutionality of
the regulating states’ laws is in deep tension with the
long-recognized principle that “the States [are]
laboratories for devising solutions to difficult legal
problems.”  Arizona State Legis . v. Arizona Indep.
Redistricting Comm ’n, 576 U.S. 787, 817 (2015)
(citations omitted).
In the end, the percentage of states restricting
AR-15s is higher than the percentage of Americans
owning AR-15s.  So, AR-15 regulation is more common
than the gun itself.

18
3. AR-15s are unusually dangerous.
Multiple courts and parties have documented the
horrors that AR -15s have visited on American
communities and schoolchildren.  See, e.g. , Cargill,
602 U.S. at 429 –430 (Sotomayor, J., dissenting);
Bianchi, 111 F. 4th at 456 –58; Viramontes Opp. to
Pet. at 1 –5; Grant Opp. to Pet. at 1 ; Grant Pet. App.
44a–45a.  The “[m]ass shootings,” enabled by AR-15s
“continue to be a growing threat unlike anything that
the Framers could have imagined. ”  Grant Pet. App.
44a.
The reason why so many perpetrators of mass
violence prefer these weapons is obvious: they are
extraordinarily lethal.  See generally Bianchi, 111 F.
4th 454–56; Grant Resp. Br. 24–28; Viramontes Resp.
Br. 28–31.  Bullets from AR-15s are about three times
faster than those from handguns, and the effective
range of AR -15s is eight to ten times greater than
those of handguns.  Grant Resp. Br. 24 –25 (citations
omitted).  The wounds AR-15s create are significantly
more devastating than those of handguns.  Id. at 25
(citations omitted).
AR-15s are much easier to fire accurately with
rapid fire than are traditional rifles.  Grant Resp. Br.
26.  AR -15s have lower recoil than hunting rifles,
allowing a shooter to easily resight and to continue
firing.  Id.  (citations omitted).  And  AR-15s are
designed to accept detachable magazines, which can
be extended to contain 30 or even 100 rounds.  Id.  at
27–28 (citations omitted).  By contrast, hunting rifles
typically “ have a fixed internal magazine that can
hold only three to five rounds .”  Id. at 27.  All of the
above is true even of a stock AR-15; its lethality only

19
increases when an end user modifies one with a bump
stock, auto sear, or forced-reset trigger.
Petitioners’ attempt to compare AR -15s to “ nonbanned rifles that are more traditionally styled ,”
Pet’rs’ Br. 16, is inapt. They first attempt to liken the
AR-15 to the less -lethal Winchester 1873 by noting
the unremarkable fact that both have stocks . See id.
So too with the unremarkable fact that both models
have grips—and different ones, at that.  Id. at 17.  And
with the fact that both guns require the shooter to use
two hands to hold it.  Id. at 19.  Each of these
attempted comparisons ignores the cluster of features
that make s AR-15s uniquely suited to mass killing.
Common sense leads to only one conclusion: these
weapons are u nusually dangerous, and the Second
Amendment does not shackle the states from
protecting its citizens against them.
CONCLUSION
This Court should affirm the judgments of the
Second and Seventh Circuits.
